title: D-006: JSON Schema for All Structured Outputs
body:
# D-006: JSON Schema for All Structured Outputs

**Date:** 2026-03-28
**Status:** Active

## Decision

Every inter-agent handoff uses a defined JSON Schema (stored in `.writing-framework/schemas/`). Agents validate outputs before delivering. Schema conflict is a defined blocker type (B7).

## Why

Without schema contracts, agents produce outputs in whatever format is convenient, and the next agent must guess the structure. This makes orchestration fragile. Schema contracts make handoffs inspectable, testable, and stable across phases.

This is the core technical enforcement of the agent-first architecture (D-001). Agent-first design requires every interface to be explicit and structured. JSON Schema is the mechanism that makes "explicit and structured" machine-enforceable rather than just a documentation convention. An agent that produces a brief in an unexpected format does not merely cause the next agent to fail — it causes a failure that is difficult to diagnose because the problem appears at the consuming agent, not the producing agent. With schema validation at the point of production, failures are caught early and attributed correctly.

Schemas defined in Phase 1: brief, outline, research_report, review_report, rewrite_plan, merge_report, blocker_report, artifact_manifest, sync_manifest, quality_gate. These ten schemas cover every structured handoff in the production pipeline.

## Alternatives Considered

**Informal conventions documented in agent specs.** Rejected: informal conventions drift and cannot be validated. Over time, "the brief output looks like this" notes in agent specs become stale, agents develop variant formats, and the orchestrator cannot reliably consume handoffs without per-agent special-casing.

**Runtime type checking only.** Rejected: runtime checking catches failures at the consuming agent. Schema validation at the producing agent catches failures at the point of production, where the fix is easier and the attribution is clearer.

## Consequences

Implementing an agent requires understanding its input and output schemas. Schema changes require a migration note and increment the schema version. Schema validation is part of the quality gate in each phase. If an agent produces an output that fails schema validation, it must classify this as a B7 (schema_conflict) blocker and apply the standard blockage protocol — it must not deliver a non-compliant output and hope the consuming agent handles it gracefully.
